title: the weapons
hook: the morning after the forest is freed, the sage hands over everything he has

segments.voice: Yesterday: Tataka, part two. Rama obeyed a promise, tried to disarm before he destroyed, and the forest was freed. Did you try the gentlest step that would work? Day five hundred two.

They spend the night in the freed forest. In the morning, Vishvamitra is smiling. He has been watching this boy. He's seen him ask before acting, obey without sulking, try mercy before force. And now the sage does something extraordinary. He decides to hand over everything he has. Not land, not gold. Something no treasury holds, and no army could take from him. He tells Rama to sit down and get ready.
screen: `THE SAGE HAS BEEN WATCHING.` → `MERCY BEFORE FORCE.` → `NOW, EVERYTHING HE HAS.`

segments.voice: What Vishvamitra gives are the astras, the divine weapons. An astra isn't just an arrow. It's a power called up by a mantra and released through a weapon: the force of a god, carried on a word. The sage names them one after another, and the list goes on for verses. The discus of dharma and the discus of time. Indra's thunderbolt. Shiva's trident. The weapon of Brahma himself. The noose of Varuna, lord of the waters. The fire weapon, the wind weapon, and one called manava, named for Manu, the first human. As Vishvamitra recites, something strange happens. The weapons appear. Not as metal, but as beings, shining, with bodies of their own, standing before Rama with their palms joined. They say: we are yours. Tell us what to do. And Rama, still a young man, touches each one with his hand and answers simply: stay in my mind, and come when I need you. Notice what the text is saying. The weapons aren't things. They're servants with their own presence, and they bow to a person, not just a skill. And notice when they're given. Not on day one. After a test. After the sage has seen how this young man uses force when force is put in his hands. In the Ramayana, power follows character. It doesn't come first.
screen: `AN ASTRA: A GOD'S POWER ON A WORD.` · `DISCUS, THUNDERBOLT, TRIDENT, NOOSE.` · `THE WEAPONS APPEAR, PALMS JOINED.` · `POWER FOLLOWS CHARACTER.` · then, large: `STAY IN MY MIND.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of one strength you have: a skill, a voice people listen to, money, patience, quickness with words. Picture it standing in front of you, palms joined, waiting. Don't send it anywhere yet. Just ask it, the way Rama did, to stay in your mind and come when it's truly needed. Breathe with that, a strength held in reserve. The bell holds the time.
The weapons. The astras, divine powers Vishvamitra gives Rama after Tataka, which appear as shining beings and wait on his mind.
Your line: the weapons. Today, hold back one strength you'd normally use, a sharp reply, a winning argument, and keep it in your mind for when it's really needed. Day five hundred two.

howItsDone: In the epics, astras are given by teachers or gods to those judged worthy, invoked by mantra; Hindu storytellers often use the gift to Rama to teach that power should follow character.

fork.setup: you're Rama. dozens of divine weapons stand before you as beings, palms joined, asking what to do. what do you tell them?

fork.reveal: he touches them and asks them to stay in his mind until needed. power held in reserve.

original.note: Sanskrit astra: a weapon that is released or hurled, in the epics a divine power called up by mantra.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rama gets magic arrows.
what it means: he's entrusted with powers that appear as beings and serve a person they trust.

what a scholar hears: Bala Kanda 27 lists the astras, from the dharma-chakra and kala-chakra to the brahmastra, the varuna-pasha and the manava; here the astras take bodily form and address Rama, and in the next sarga the withdrawals do the same.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 27 (the gift of the astras; the weapons appear as beings)

notes: The list of astras is abridged to ones the script is confident appear in Bala Kanda 27 (dharma-chakra, kala-chakra, Indra's vajra, Shiva's trident, brahmastra, varuna-pasha, agneya, vayavya, manava). Confirm each.
'Facing east' for receiving the weapons: confirm the text's detail.
'Power follows character' is the script's reading, not a quotation.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut 'two days', 'ages of austerity', 'kings and gods would give anything' and 'face east' (not confirmed in Bala Kanda 27); 'teenager' became 'young man'; the trapdoor no longer calls the embodied weapons unique to this scene, since day 503 has the withdrawals take form too.
